name: similarity-ratio-table
title: Similar shapes scale-factor table
tagline: Length, Area and Volume scale-factor table (k, k², k³); one factor back-derives the others exactly with surds; cells occlude for complete-the-table.
description: A canonical working table for the similar-shapes scale-factor relationship: Length SF = k, Area SF = k², Volume SF = k³, shown as three columns with a symbolic power row (k, k², k³) above the numeric scale-factor row. You give exactly one scale factor — the length SF k, the area SF (k²) or the volume SF (k³) — and the model back-derives k and the other two exactly: k = the value, √(area SF) or ∛(volume SF), then k² and k³. Non-integer factors stay exact (k = 1.5 → 9⁄4 → 27⁄8 i.e. 2.25, 3.375) and an irrational k renders as a real surd (area SF 2 → k = √2 → volume SF 2√2; volume SF 10 → k = ∛10 → area SF ∛100). Occlude any value cell to "?" for "complete the table" / "given the area ratio, find the volume ratio", highlight the answer in amber, and switch on the working strip to show how k is found and substituted. The tabular, numeric partner to the geometry/similar-shapes figure.
whenToUse: Reach for this for the similar-shapes scale-factor relationship as a table: length scale factor k, area scale factor k², volume scale factor k³ — "given any one, find the others". Author the one scale factor you are given with given { of: "length" | "area" | "volume", value }: of "length" gives k directly (forward — find the area and volume factors); of "area" gives the area SF and the model finds k = √(area SF) (reverse — "area ratio → length / volume ratio"); of "volume" gives the volume SF and the model finds k = ∛(volume SF). Everything else — k, k², k³, every cell, the widths — is derived, so you never write a derived factor. The common questions: complete the table / forward — given.of "length" (k known), occlude: { area: true, volume: true } for the answer space; area → volume (the classic) — given.of "area", occlude: { length: true, volume: true }, optionally highlight: { volume: true } on the answer; volume → area — given.of "volume", occlude length and area; find the scale factor — given.of "area" or "volume", occlude: { length: true } (k is the unknown). Switch show.working on for a worked example (it reveals the find-k step "k = √9 = 3" and the substitutions "k³ = 3³ = 27"); the working is occlusion-aware, so on an occluded question it shows "?" for the hidden value rather than leaking it. show.powers (default on) is the k / k² / k³ reference row — keep it on while teaching the relationship, off for a bare recall table. show.volume false drops the volume column for a length-and-area-only lesson (forced on when given.of is volume). Keep the same orientation and the powers row consistent across a lesson. Surds: an area SF that is not a perfect square gives a surd k (area SF 2 → √2, area SF 8 → 2√2) and a surd volume SF — the cells and working render the real radicals. Switch primitive when the teaching changes — to draw the two similar figures with marked corresponding sides and a × k arrow use geometry/similar-shapes; for an enlargement about a centre on a grid use geometry/transformations; for a single 3D solid's volume / surface area use geometry/solid. Synonyms a teacher might use: similar shapes scale factor, length area volume scale factor, LSF ASF VSF, area ratio, volume ratio, ratio of areas, ratio of volumes, k squared k cubed, area scale factor, volume scale factor, scale factor table, complete the table, find the volume scale factor.

given.description: The ONE scale factor you are given — the single stimulus of the question. The model back-derives k and the other two factors from it, so this is the only number you author.

of.description: Which scale factor `value` is. "length" = the linear scale factor k itself (forward case); "area" = the area scale factor k² (the model finds k = √value); "volume" = the volume scale factor k³ (the model finds k = ∛value).

value.description: The numeric scale factor named by `of`, a positive number. e.g. of "length" value 3 → areas ×9, volumes ×27; of "area" value 9 → k = 3; of "volume" value 8 → k = 2. Non-integers stay exact (length 1.5 → area 2.25, volume 3.375); an area that is not a perfect square gives a surd k (area 2 → √2).

occlude.description: Per-dimension Render the value as "?" (the question hook) for. Address a value by its dimension: length (= k), area (= k²) or volume (= k³). The power row (k, k², k³) and the column headers are never affected.

length.description: Render the value as "?" (the question hook) for the Length SF value (k).

area.description: Render the value as "?" (the question hook) for the Area SF value (k²).

volume.description: Render the value as "?" (the question hook) for the Volume SF value (k³).

highlight.description: Per-dimension Amber the value (answer emphasis) for. Address a value by its dimension: length (= k), area (= k²) or volume (= k³). The power row (k, k², k³) and the column headers are never affected.

length.description: Amber the value (answer emphasis) for the Length SF value (k).

area.description: Amber the value (answer emphasis) for the Area SF value (k²).

volume.description: Amber the value (answer emphasis) for the Volume SF value (k³).

powers.description: Show the symbolic power row k / k² / k³ above the numeric scale factors — the relationship reference. Default true; set false for a bare recall table of just the numbers.

working.description: Show the derivation strip beneath the table: how k is found (e.g. "k = √9 = 3" or "k = ∛8 = 2") and the substitutions for the other factors ("Area SF = k² = 3² = 9"). Occlusion-aware — a hidden value shows "?" in the working too, so it never leaks. Use on worked examples. Default false.

volume.description: Show the Volume SF (k³) column. Default true. Set false for a length-and-area-only lesson (length and area are always shown). Forced true when given.of is "volume".

header.description: Optional short title centred above the table; the top padding grows to clear it.

caption.description: Optional line centred below the table, e.g. a short context note. Never the question or an instruction: that wording is the block's text.
